node-1.label: A man in his 40s presented with a 3-month history of discrete, dark red, circular lesions in his right axilla

node-2.label: He endorsed severe pruritus at these sites that would wake him up at night; denied recent trauma, similar lesions, pain, blisters, or systemic symptoms (fever, chills).

node-3.label: His medical history was unremarkable; no environmental triggers or new medications; treatment with over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream, ketoconazole cream, and discontinuation of underarm deodorant yielded no improvement.

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed 3 well-circumscribed, violaceous, annular patches without scale or erosion limited to the right axilla; no other lesions on skin or mucous membranes; Wood lamp examination was negative.

why.why: Both the Pathologist and Laboratory Physician explicitly favor an inflammatory dermatosis over infection or granulomatous disease, and the H&E finding of lymphocytes obscuring the dermal-epidermal junction supports a lymphocytic interface process. However, immunophenotyping and TCR gene rearrangement remain unavailable, so the diagnosis is not fully confirmed; confidence is raised to 0.55.

The Pathologist's analysis favors inflammatory dermatosis over infection, and the Laboratory Physician's assessment likewise supports inflammation rather than infection. Combined with the negative Wood lamp examination, absence of scale, and failed ketoconazole treatment, fungal skin infection is very unlikely; confidence is lowered to 0.03.

Both expert analyses continue to emphasize that cutaneous lymphoma cannot be excluded because immunophenotyping, TCR gene rearrangement, flow cytometry, DIF, and autoimmune serologies are absent. The Laboratory Physician additionally notes that systemic imaging remains unavailable, further extending the incomplete workup. Clinical features favor an inflammatory process, but the unresolved confirmatory data and inability to stage keep lymphoma a significant differential; confidence remains moderate at 0.35.

The Pathologist favors inflammatory dermatosis over granulomatous disease, and the Laboratory Physician finds granulomatous dermatosis less likely because severe pruritus is atypical and the biopsy shows lymphocytes obscuring the dermal-epidermal junction rather than granulomas. Confidence is reduced to 0.07.
